conditions.manipulation_text: The shift supervisor strongly suspects that the operator opened PV-101 incorrectly and caused the pressure loss. Test this hypothesis against all available evidence.

evidence_items.text: During the pressure decrease, PV-101 received a closing command, but local valve-position inspection found it remained open.
The available operator action log contains no manual opening command to PV-101 during the observed event window.
An independent pressure indication corroborated the pressure decrease; the inspected line segment showed no visible external leak, but a complete line-integrity test was not available.

surface_forms.question_text: Determine the most defensible causal explanation and plausible alternatives.

case_payload.title: Low pressure with PV-101 remaining open

surface_form_payload.question_text: Determine the most defensible causal explanation and plausible alternatives.

candidate_causes.cause_description: PV-101 failed to close on command. The final control element stuck or failed open (trim/stem binding, actuator, positioner/I-P or actuator air supply; specific mode undetermined). This left open the path whose closure was the commanded pressure-restoring action, allowing continued depressurisation of V-001 and the crude input line.

evidence_against.relevance: E1 does not show when or why PV-101 was open, whether it moved open spuriously (initiator) or only failed to arrest a decrease begun elsewhere, or which failure mode applies.
No complete line-integrity test was available, so a concurrent contributing leak is not excluded; PV-101 may not be the sole cause.

evidence_for.relevance: A closing command was issued during the pressure decrease, yet local inspection verified PV-101 remained open. This is direct, physically confirmed failure of the final control element to respond. Since closure was the commanded pressure-restoring action, the open valve is consistent with sustained depressurisation.
An independent indication confirms a genuine process pressure decrease rather than a measurement artefact, consistent with inventory loss through an open PV-101.
No manual opening command is logged, so the open state is not attributable to recorded operator input, which points to an equipment malfunction.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Loss of containment from V-001 or associated lines through a leak outside the inspected segment or below visual detectability. This would reduce inventory and pressure, alone or concurrently with the PV-101 failure.

evidence_against.relevance: The inspected line segment showed no visible external leak.
The verified open PV-101 already supplies a directly observed depressurisation path, reducing the explanatory need for an unobserved leak.

evidence_for.relevance: The decrease is corroborated as real and no complete line-integrity test was available, so a leak outside the inspected segment or below visual detectability is not excluded.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Reduced crude supply or upstream inlet pressure to the input line initiated the pressure decrease. In this case PV-101's failure to close was a failed control response that prevented recovery, not the initiator.

evidence_against.relevance: A verified equipment malfunction that alone can sustain depressurisation reduces the need to posit an unobserved upstream change.
The corroboration concerns pressure only. The packet contains no inlet flow, upstream pressure or supply-side data supporting a supply reduction.

evidence_for.relevance: The deviation spans the crude input line as well as V-001. This pattern is compatible with a supply-side reduction as well as with downstream venting through PV-101.
The closing command is consistent with a controller responding to falling pressure whose origin could lie upstream. PV-101's failure would then explain non-recovery rather than initiation.

candidate_causes.cause_description: Unlogged manual operator action opening PV-101 or otherwise lowering pressure. This is assessed only to test it against the record; no evidence of any such action exists.

evidence_against.relevance: No manual opening command to PV-101 is recorded during the event window.
PV-101 was commanded to close, the pressure-restoring direction, yet stayed open. The anomaly lies in the valve's response, not in any command issued.

evidence_for.relevance: The record is described only as the 'available' log and its completeness is not confirmed. This documentary gap, not any positive evidence, is the sole basis for a residual allocation.

parsed_response.concise_technical_rationale: HAZOP framing: the node is V-001 and associated lines. The implied design intent is to hold operating pressure, with PV-101 as the final control element (a pressure-control valve by tag convention; its location and fail position are not stated). Guideword LOW/LESS is applied to pressure. The deviation is real: an independent indication corroborates the decrease (E3), effectively excluding a false low reading. The only directly evidenced malfunction is PV-101 failing to close on command during the decrease, confirmed by local position inspection (E1). Because closure was the commanded pressure-restoring action, the open valve sufficiently explains sustained depressurisation and is ranked primary (72%). No manual opening command is logged (E2), so operator error is not inferred; it receives only a 2% residual reflecting unverified log completeness. A leak is weakened (no visible leak on the inspected segment) but not excluded (no complete integrity test). An upstream supply reduction is neither supported nor excluded by packet data. Either could have initiated the decrease, with PV-101's failure then preventing recovery (13% each). Reference consequences are depressurisation, material damage, generator stop, inability to discharge V-001 and unit shutdown. No safeguards are listed (CASE-04), so no credited layer is identified to arrest escalation from a single final-element failure. The qualitative priority is high, although likelihood cannot be calibrated from the packet. Recommendations: diagnose and stroke-test PV-101 (trim/stem, actuator, positioner, air supply); add valve-position feedback with a command-discrepancy alarm; add an independent V-001 low-pressure alarm/trip; complete line-integrity testing; review upstream inlet flow/pressure trends; and confirm operator/DCS log completeness.
uncertainty_notes: The packet does not state PV-101's location, service or fail-safe position, or whether the closing command was automatic or manual. The interpretation relies on E1, where closure was the commanded pressure-restoring action, and on tag convention.
No timing of PV-101 travel relative to the pressure trend is provided. E1 therefore cannot show whether PV-101 initiated the decrease or only failed to arrest a decrease that started elsewhere.
The PV-101 failure mode (trim/stem binding, actuator, positioner/I-P, actuator air supply or signal) is undetermined; valve diagnostics are required.
No complete line-integrity test was available, so a leak outside the inspected segment or below visual detectability is not excluded (E3).
The packet contains no upstream crude supply flow or pressure data, so an upstream supply reduction is neither supported nor excluded.
The operator log is described only as the 'available' log and its completeness is not confirmed. No operator action has been inferred.
The source-derived cause list is withheld (CASE-05) and no safeguards are listed (CASE-04). The candidate set may differ from the reference, and the risk priority is qualitative only.
Latent or organisational causes (maintenance, testing, loop design) are not evidenced, so the assessment stops at the direct equipment-failure level.

I'm examining the low pressure event in the crude input line and separator V-001, focusing on the evidence that PV-101 received a close command but was found still open during inspection—pointing to a possible stuck valve, actuator failure, positioner malfunction, or loss of instrument air.

I'm checking whether operator error could explain this: the action log shows no manual opening command during the event window, so that possibility isn't supported, though I note the log could theoretically be incomplete. I'm also weighing whether this is a real process deviation versus a false instrument reading—an independent pressure indication confirms the pressure drop is genuine, and while no external leak was found in the inspected segment, a full line-integrity test wasn't performed, so a leak elsewhere isn't fully ruled out. This leads me to identify PV-101's mechanical failure to close as the leading candidate cause, supported by both the command-response mismatch and the corroborated pressure drop.

I'm now considering causal direction—whether the stuck valve caused the depressurization or whether some other unknown upstream trigger started it and the valve simply failed to correct it. If PV-101 vents gas from V-001, a closing command on falling pressure would be the expected control response, so its failure to close would indeed explain continued depressurization, but I have no data on feed flow or upstream conditions, so I shouldn't speculate beyond what's given. I'm also considering a second candidate: a fault in the control signal path itself, where the closing command was generated but never properly transmitted to or executed by the valve.

This suggests splitting into two distinct candidates—mechanical failure of the valve/actuator versus instrumentation or signal failure in the control loop—since the evidence can't discriminate between them, and I need to decide whether to allocate probability across both rather than picking one as primary.

The wording "received a closing command" leans toward the signal reaching the valve, which would point more toward the failure being local to the valve assembly itself—mechanical, actuator, or positioner-related—rather than upstream in the signal path, though I should flag this as an interpretive assumption rather than certain fact.

I should also weigh other candidate causes: air supply loss (but fail-safe position is unknown, so I shouldn't assume), external leak or containment loss (weak evidence, no visible leak found, maybe 10% plausibility), and reduced upstream crude supply (E3's pressure drop could support this, but there's no direct evidence about upstream conditions, so I need to be careful not to invent facts not in the packet).

Since the crude input line and V-001 are connected, a depressurization at V-001 would naturally propagate upstream too — so the low pressure reading there is actually consistent with E1's equipment failure explanation rather than requiring a separate upstream cause.

Actually this connectivity also complicates things: if PV-101 is a back-pressure controller, the closing command in E1 might just be the automatic control response trying to counteract the pressure drop, not the initiating event itself. That reframes the question of whether the valve staying open is the original fault or a failed corrective action.

The inspection only notes the valve "remained open" without specifying degree, so it's genuinely ambiguous whether PV-101 was the initiating cause (failed open due to actuator/positioner/air fault) or simply a secondary failure that didn't correct an already-developing pressure drop.

Either way, PV-101's failure to close on demand is the most defensible primary cause with direct evidence, though I need to avoid inventing details about its service or location since the packet doesn't specify these—only that "PV" conventionally denotes a pressure control valve.

Considering operator error as a candidate too: the log shows no manual opening command, but completeness isn't verified, so I'm weighing whether to include this with a small residual plausibility (3-5%) rather than dismissing it entirely, while being careful not to infer an operator action the evidence doesn't support.

My conclusion: operator_error_is_primary should be false, with PV-101's mechanical/instrumentation failure as the primary cause, and contradictory_evidence_was_considered should be true since I'm explicitly weighing evidence against the operator-error hypothesis rather than ignoring it.

I could cite E1 as weak indirect evidence for operator error—an open PV-101 matches what an erroneous manual open would look like, though E1 actually attributes it to failure-to-respond rather than any operator input—and E2 as evidence against. I lean toward keeping operator error in the candidate list at low plausibility (2-3%) with an honest note that nothing substantively supports it, rather than excluding it outright, since a thorough root cause analysis should enumerate and discount rather than omit.

I should avoid inferring any operator action not grounded in the record, including things like a controller left in manual with an operator-held output. Turning to another candidate, a false-high reading from PT-101 upstream of the valve doesn't fit either, since E1 confirms PV-101 received a legitimate closing command, meaning the controller itself was behaving correctly.

Given that, a fault in the signal or actuation path—like the I/P converter, positioner, instrument air, or wiring—failing to execute that closing command lines up much better with E1. As for a false low-pressure indication, E3's independent corroborating measurement makes that unlikely, though I could still list it at very low plausibility just to show I considered the contradictory evidence.

Actually, I'll leave the false-indication idea out of the candidates since there's no real evidence for it — instead I'll just note in the rationale that E3 rules out a purely instrumented false low-pressure reading. Now I'm reconsidering whether "upstream feed reduction" deserves its own candidate given the packet context about the crude input line and separator vessel.

Since low inlet flow/pressure from wells is a standard HAZOP cause for this deviation, it's a plausible alternative even without direct evidence, and listing it isn't inventing facts as long as I flag the lack of evidence. I'll give it a modest weight around 10%, since the packet neither confirms nor rules it out and it's consistent with the closing command.

I'm also considering internal leakage paths like a passing valve, open bypass, or a lifting relief valve — but these would require an equipment failure or operator action that isn't documented in the evidence provided.

Since the inspected segment shows no visible leak but a full integrity test wasn't performed, I'm bundling this into a candidate for loss of containment from V-001 or associated lines outside the inspected area, giving it roughly 10% plausibility. Then I start listing the main failure candidates: C1 covers a mechanical failure of the PV-101 valve/actuator assembly itself at around 45% plausibility, while C2 covers a failure in the actuation or control signal path, like the positioner.

I'm weighing whether to split C1 and C2 or merge them, since the evidence can't really discriminate between a mechanical failure and an instrumentation failure — both could explain the valve failing to close on command. rendered_system_prompt:
You are an independent process-safety specialist conducting a single-pass HAZOP judgment for a controlled research experiment.

Use only the information supplied in the case packet. Do not invent plant facts, operating data, safeguards, incident histories, or causal evidence. Where the packet is insufficient, state the uncertainty explicitly. Apply the HAZOP logic of design intent, guideword/deviation, cause, consequence, safeguard, qualitative risk classification, and recommendation.

The risk matrix is qualitative and is intended for prioritization rather than quantitative risk calculation. Provide a concise evidence-oriented technical rationale; do not provide private chain-of-thought or a step-by-step hidden reasoning transcript. Return exactly one response conforming to the required structured-output schema, with no text outside that structure.
rendered_user_prompt:
# Isolated experiment event
Event ID: event__confirmation__CONF-LOWPRESSURE-01__control__direct__r0
Task family: root-cause assessment

# Source-grounded process context
[CASE-01] Node: V-001 and associated lines.
[CASE-02] Element and deviation: Pressure — Low pressure in the crude input line and separator vessel V-001.
[CASE-03] Potential consequences in the HAZOP reference: Depressurisation of V-001 and associated lines.; Material damage.; Stop generators.; Impossibility of discharging fluids from V-001.; Unit shutdown.
[CASE-04] Existing safeguards in the HAZOP reference: none listed
[CASE-05] The source-derived possible-cause list is withheld from the model and retained for human audit.

# Event evidence
[E1] During the pressure decrease, PV-101 received a closing command, but local valve-position inspection found it remained open.
[E2] The available operator action log contains no manual opening command to PV-101 during the observed event window.
[E3] An independent pressure indication corroborated the pressure decrease; the inspected line segment showed no visible external leak, but a complete line-integrity test was not available.

# Task
Perform a neutral root-cause assessment.
Determine the most defensible causal explanation and plausible alternatives.

Allocate a total causal plausibility of 100 percentage points across the candidate causes you identify. For every candidate, cite evidence for and against it. Do not infer an operator action that is absent from the evidence record.
